children: By Nate Raymond

A federal appeals court on Tuesday concluded that a mostly undisclosed decades-long friendship between a U.S. magistrate judge and a lawyer warranted wiping out an almost $125 million judgment the judge had issued against a Louisiana industrial port.
In a

, the New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said that now-former U.S. Magistrate Judge Kathleen Kay had disclosed to the parties in the case only that the daughter of the plaintiff's lead attorney was a law clerk and left out the extent of their relationship.

"At best, this disclosure was incomplete," U.S. Circuit Judge James Graves wrote for the majority. He said Kay had been close family friends for nearly 40 years with the lead attorney for IFG Port Holdings, which had sued the Port of Lake Charles, Louisiana, as part of a complex contract dispute.

Graves said that "vanishingly little direct or circumstantial evidence suggests the Port actually knew about the friendship," undermining its ability to consent to having the case heard by a magistrate judge rather than a life-tenured district court judge.
"Judge Kay’s actions raise serious concerns about the fairness of her proceedings," Graves wrote. "Her unusually harsh order, coupled with the windfall verdict, exacerbates this impression."

U.S. Circuit Judge Andrew Oldham dissented, saying the majority's ruling awards a "Hail Mary pass" by the port to overturn the judgment, "encourages parties to scrutinize judges’ private affairs, and jeopardizes virtually all magistrate and bankruptcy judge orders."

"Recall the facts," Oldham wrote. "The Port’s lawyers repeatedly searched for a legitimate, on-the-merits way out of this judgment. And after exhausting all legally meritorious options, they were able to overturn a $112 million judgment based primarily on wedding photos from the 1980s."
Lawyers for the parties did not respond to requests for comment. Kay, who retired in December 2023, could not be reached for comment.

The case involved a years-long contract dispute between IFG Port Holdings and the port over who was responsible for securing permitting to dredge part of the Contraband Bayou so IFG could develop an export grain terminal.
Following a non-jury trial, Kay in 2019 awarded IFG $124.5 million.
But the port's lawyers said they later learned Kay was longtime family friends with IFG's lead attorney, William Monk of Stockwell, Sievert, Viccellio, Clements & Shaddock.

While Kay had disclosed that Monk's daughter clerked for her, IFG said it was never told that Monk had also been the groomsman at Kay's wedding and that the judge officiated his daughter's wedding a few months before IFG filed its case in 2016.

A district court judge had initially declined to toss the award. After the 5th Circuit ordered an inquiry into the matter in September 2023, a lower-court judge held a three-day evidentiary hearing and ruled in the port's favor.
The case is IFG Port Holdings v. Lake Charles Harbor & Terminal District, 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, No. 22-30398.
For IFG Port Holdings: Gregory Garre of Latham & Watkins
For Port of Lake Charles: Michael Rubin of McGlinchey Stafford
